presentation.history_of_present_illness: Patient presents to urgent care with a severe headache that began approximately 8 hours ago while sitting at his desk. He describes the pain as 'like someone flipped a switch,' reaching 10/10 intensity almost immediately. The headache is diffuse, with prominent occipital pain extending into his neck, and has remained severe since onset. He describes it as the worst headache he has ever experienced. He vomited twice shortly after the headache began and reports persistent nausea and sensitivity to light. He has experienced occasional mild headaches in the past but nothing similar to this episode. He took ibuprofen 600 mg without significant relief. He denies fever, recent head trauma, focal weakness, numbness, or visual loss.

relevant_context: Reports increased occupational stress and poor sleep over the preceding week
No known family history of intracranial aneurysm

exam.general: Uncomfortable appearing, sitting in a darkened examination room. No acute cardiopulmonary distress.
exam.neurologic: Alert and oriented. Speech fluent. Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements intact. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial strength and sensation symmetric. Strength 5/5 throughout. Sensation intact to light touch. Finger-to-nose testing normal. Gait steady. No focal neurologic deficits. Neck movement is limited by pain, with resistance to passive neck flexion.

benchmarks_rationale.Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Mandatory rule-out. Thunderclap onset peaking under 1 minute carries high initial mortality; immediate non-contrast head CT +/- LP is non-negotiable.
benchmarks_rationale.Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syn: Diagnostic breadth/extra credit. Important vascular differential in thunderclap presentation, often triggered by exertion or Valsalva, but missing this does not indicate an unsafe triage if SAH is pursued.
benchmarks_rationale.Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis: Diagnostic breadth. Can present with thunderclap or acute severe headache with elevated pressure signs.
benchmarks_rationale.Cervical Artery Dissection: Diagnostic breadth. May present with acute occipital/neck pain after exertion or straining.

key_evidence: Headache reached maximum intensity almost immediately
First episode of headache of this severity and character
Persistent severe diffuse headache with prominent occipital and neck pain
Neck movement limited by pain with resistance to passive flexion

required_actions: Identify subarachnoid hemorrhage as the leading suspected diagnosis
Recommend immediate emergency department transfer for evaluation of suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage
Recommend urgent noncontrast CT of the head
Recommend lumbar puncture following a negative noncontrast CT when indicated, particularly given presentation approximately 8 hours after onset and persistent high clinical suspicion
Recognize that a normal focal neurologic examination does not exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage
contraindicated_actions: Diagnose uncomplicated migraine or another primary headache disorder without urgent evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage
Discharge the patient without emergency evaluation
Recommend routine outpatient neuroimaging instead of immediate emergency evaluation
Use absence of focal neurologic deficits to exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage
Recommend symptomatic headache treatment alone without investigating the thunderclap onset
acceptable_actions: Arrange emergency medical transport and monitor neurologic status during transfer
Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetic treatment without delaying emergency evaluation
Recommend CT angiography or other vascular imaging when clinically indicated
Recommend urgent neurosurgical or neurovascular consultation if subarachnoid hemorrhage is confirmed
Consider alternative secondary thunderclap headache etiologies if the initial subarachnoid hemorrhage evaluation is negative
